blocks.text: Pliny, book 11, chapter 18: They carry out the dead, and accompany the obsequies in the manner of mourners. Aelian, Historia, book 5, chapter 49: Χελιδὼν ἐκβάλλει χελιδόνα νεκρὰν, καὶ μέλιτταν μέλιττα· [Chelidōn ekballei chelidona nekran, kai melittan melitta] A swallow carries out a dead swallow, and a bee a bee. Damir: اذا هلك شي منها داخل الخلايا اخرجته الاحيا خارج [idhā halaka shay minhā dākhil al-khalāyā akhrajathu al-aḥyā khārij] When one of them has died in the hive, the living carry it outside. [III, 356] To these objections that can be raised against the sacred text I have two answers. First, the bees were found in the lion's body, but were not born there; for the author does not assert this. Those therefore are mistaken who on this basis posit a race of bees λεοντογενῶν [leontogenōn], since nowhere in the writings of the ancients do we read that bees are born from a lion. Nor should we listen to Moffett, the Englishman, who in the Insectorum Theatrum writes that some bees are λεοντογενεῖς [leontogeneis], others ταυρογενεῖς [taurogeneis]: namely, that the best and truly noble ones have their origin from the lion, and that their princes and kings derive their lineage from its brain. Hence, he says, it comes about that, small as they are, they sometimes attack the very largest animals and, endowed with leonine ferocity, fear nothing. If this were true, bees would be fiercest in places that teem with lions. But I shall prove without any trouble that the matter is quite otherwise. For in Ethiopia, where Oppian, in book 3 of the Cynegetica, describes those terrible lions from personal observation, bees are so tame that they usually build their nests among the dwellings of men. So Alvarez testifies in his Ethiopia. On the other hand, in Crete ^{a)}, where there are neither lions, nor wolves, nor bears, nor any harmful animal, bees were so fierce that they sometimes drove the inhabitants from their homes, as will be proved below. And in Scythia ^{b)}, which is very far from lions, certain places beyond the Ister were once inaccessible, because bees so occupied them that one could not advance further. Herodotus, book 5, chapter 10, reports that he received this from the Thracians, who live nearest the Ister. He himself, however, rejects it as hardly credible, on the ground that bees seem to be ζῶα δύσριγα [zōa dysriga], animals that cannot endure cold. But many writers refute Herodotus: thus Maximus of Tyre, Oration 2 On Love: Σκυθῶν δὲ οἱ μὲν πολλοὶ γάλακτι βιοτεύουσιν, ὡς οἱ ἄλλοι ἐπὶ οἴνῳ, τοῖς δὲ αἱ μέλιτται καθηδύνουσι τὸ πόμα, ἐπὶ πετρῶν καὶ δρυῶν διαπλάττουσαι τοὺς σίμβλους. [Skythōn de hoi men polloi galakti bioteuousin, hōs hoi alloi epi oinō, tois de hai melittai kathēdynousi to poma, epi petrōn kai dryōn diaplattousai tous simblous.] Most of the Scythians sustain life on milk, just as others do on wine; for others, the bees, which build their honeycombs either on rocks or in oaks, sweeten their drink. And Aelian, book 2, ch. 53: I remember that someone records [col. 505] καὶ μελίττας Σκυθίδας εἶναι, ἐπαΐειν τε τοῦ κρύους οὐδὲν, καὶ μέν τοι καὶ πιπράσκειν εἰς Μυσοὺς κομίζοντας Σκύθας, οὐκ ἐθνεῖον (read ὀθνεῖον) σφίσιν, ἀλλ᾽ ἀνθιγενὲς (read αὐθιγενὲς) μέλι καὶ κηρία ἐπιχώρια [kai melittas Skythidas einai, epaiein te tou kryous ouden, kai men toi kai pipraskein eis Mysous komizontas Skythas, ouk ethneion (read othneion) sphisin, alla anthigenes (read authigenes) meli kai kēria epichōria], that there are bees also in Scythia which are not harmed by the cold, and that the Scythians export honey, not foreign but native, and native honeycombs, for sale to the Mysians. Nor let anyone be indignant with me for writing contrary to Herodotus. For he who writes this has declared that he is presenting history, not repeating uncertain rumour. And Matthias of Miechów, book 2 On European Sarmatia, ch. 1: This is the most fertile of lands, and most productive of grain and honey. Likewise: Swarms of bees make honey not only in hives and hollowed trees, but also deposit honey of their own accord in trees and in the earth. [III, 357] And Paolo Giovio, in his book On the Embassy of the Muscovites: The surest harvest of Muscovy consists in wax and honey. For the whole region is full of most fertile bees, which produce the finest honey not in hives made by the hands of peasants, but in the very hollows of trees. See there the rest, about very large lakes of honey, and about the peasant who, sunk in a pool of honey, was wondrously rescued by a she-bear. For I do not care to linger longer on a very well-known matter.
